es: Reconocer quién toma, mantiene, interrumpe o cede el turno en una mesa redonda a partir de las expresiones que usa cada participante.

teaching.en: The moderator opened the panel by asking each guest in turn to state one priority for the coming year.
teaching.es: La moderadora abrió la mesa pidiendo a cada invitado, por turno, que dijera una prioridad para el año que viene.
teaching.explanationEs: In turn indica un orden: uno tras otro, sin que dos hablen a la vez.
segments: The moderator opened the panel by asking each guest in
turn to state one priority for the coming year.
teaching.audioText: The moderator opened the panel by asking each guest in turn to state one priority for the coming year.

teaching.en: If I may, I would like to take the floor for a moment, since nobody has yet mentioned the cost.
teaching.es: Si me lo permite, me gustaría tomar la palabra un momento, ya que nadie ha mencionado todavía el costo.
teaching.explanationEs: Take the floor es pedir o tomar el turno; If I may lo suaviza con cortesía.
segments: If I may, I would like to take the floor
for a moment, since nobody has yet mentioned the cost.
teaching.audioText: If I may, I would like to take the floor for a moment, since nobody has yet mentioned the cost.

teaching.en: As I was saying, the cost matters, and I intend to hold the floor until I have finished this point.
teaching.es: Como decía, el costo importa, y pienso mantener la palabra hasta terminar este punto.
teaching.explanationEs: Hold the floor es retener el turno; As I was saying retoma una idea que alguien acaba de cortar.
segments: As I was saying, the cost matters, and I intend
to hold the floor until I have finished this point.
teaching.audioText: As I was saying, the cost matters, and I intend to hold the floor until I have finished this point.

teaching.en: Sorry to interrupt, but may I chime in here before the discussion moves on?
teaching.es: Perdona que interrumpa, pero ¿puedo intervenir ahora, antes de que la discusión avance?
teaching.explanationEs: Sorry to interrupt + but pide permiso con cortesía; chime in significa intervenir en una conversación ya empezada.
segments: Sorry to interrupt, but may I chime
in here before the discussion moves on?
teaching.audioText: Sorry to interrupt, but may I chime in here before the discussion moves on?

teaching.en: A fair moderator never lets one guest talk over another, and asks the louder guest to yield the floor.
teaching.es: Un buen moderador nunca deja que un invitado hable encima de otro, y pide al más ruidoso que ceda la palabra.
teaching.explanationEs: Talk over es hablar mientras otro habla; yield the floor es lo que debe hacer quien no respeta el turno.
segments: A fair moderator never lets one guest talk over another,
and asks the louder guest to yield the floor.
teaching.audioText: A fair moderator never lets one guest talk over another, and asks the louder guest to yield the floor.

teaching.en: That is all from me; I will hand over to the moderator, and then Leo may go ahead with his reply.
teaching.es: Eso es todo por mi parte; cedo la palabra a la moderadora, y después Leo podrá responder.
teaching.explanationEs: Hand over to + persona cede el turno; go ahead invita a empezar a quien espera.
segments: That is all from me; I will hand over to the
moderator, and then Leo may go ahead with his reply.
teaching.audioText: That is all from me; I will hand over to the moderator, and then Leo may go ahead with his reply.

prompt.es: ¿Qué función de turno cumple el fragmento?

choices.text: She keeps a turn that she already holds.
She gives the turn to someone else.
She asks politely for a turn to speak.

feedback.es: «If I may» y «take the floor» piden permiso para empezar a hablar: la oradora solicita el turno.

hint.es: Fíjate en quién quiere empezar a hablar y cómo lo pide.

origin.text: If I may, I would like to take the floor for a moment, because nobody has mentioned the people who will pay for all of this.

prompt.es: Completa: «Todos respondieron por turno, sin interrupciones.»

answer.text: in

feedback.es: In turn significa «uno tras otro»; es la colocación que describe un reparto ordenado del turno.

hint.es: Es la preposición de la colocación «___ turn».

origin.text: The moderator looked at the four guests and asked each of them, in turn, for a single priority. Everyone answered ___ turn, without interruptions.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Adelante, Leo, cuéntanos qué piensas.»

answer.text: Please go ahead, Leo, and tell us what you think

feedback.es: Go ahead cede el turno a quien espera, y and tell us invita a continuar con lo que va a decir.

hint.es: Empieza con la fórmula que invita a hablar.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué hace la moderadora con el turno?

choices.text: She gives the turn to Ana and reminds her of the time.
She gives the turn to Ana and asks her to answer Carlos at length.
She promises Ana more time after the other guests have spoken.

feedback.es: Agradece a Carlos, cede la palabra a Ana y le recuerda que debe ser breve porque otros esperan.

origin.audio: Thank you, Carlos. That was clear, and I think Ana wanted to respond. Ana, the floor is yours, but please keep it brief, because we still have two guests who have not yet spoken.

prompt.es: ¿Qué hace la oradora ante la interrupción?

choices.text: She asks for a turn she does not have.
She defends the turn she already holds.
She hands the turn over to the interrupter.

feedback.es: «I have not finished» y «As I was saying» defienden el turno propio frente a la interrupción.

origin.text: Wait, I have not finished. As I was saying, cost is only one part of the problem, and if you let me explain the second part, you will see why it matters more.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con la función que cumple en la mesa.

pairs: Can I chime in here for a second?
Please, let me finish this point.
Sorry to interrupt, but I must disagree.
I will hand over to Leo now.

pairs.es: Cede el turno a otra persona

pairs: Could we hear from everyone in turn?

feedback.es: Cada frase tiene su función: entrar, retener, cortar con tacto, ceder u ordenar la palabra.

pairs: Can I chime in here for a second?
Please, let me finish this point.
Sorry to interrupt, but I must disagree.
I will hand over to Leo now.

pairs.es: Cede el turno a otra persona

pairs: Could we hear from everyone in turn?

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿por qué no pudo hablar Sara cuando intentó intervenir?

choices.text: Because the moderator told her to wait for Leo first.
Because Sara realised that her point was not relevant.
Because Tom refused to yield the floor before finishing.

feedback.es: Tom siguió hablando y dijo que no había terminado: retuvo la palabra y Sara no pudo entrar.

origin.audio: The moderator welcomed the guests and asked each of them in turn for one priority. Tom took the floor first and spoke for nearly three full minutes about cost. Halfway through, Sara tried to add a comment, but Tom carried on, saying that he had not finished. Sara sat back, clearly annoyed, while the rest of the panel waited in silence. When Tom finally handed over, the moderator thanked him, turned to Sara and said: Go ahead, but please keep it brief, because Leo has been waiting patiently for his turn.

prompt.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué da a entender la última frase de la moderadora?

choices.text: That she wants to be fair to the guest who spoke least.
That she plans to give Tom a second chance to speak afterwards.
That she hopes the panel will end a little earlier than planned.

feedback.es: Al pedir brevedad por Leo, que espera desde hace rato, deja ver su interés en repartir la palabra con justicia.

origin.audio: The moderator welcomed the guests and asked each of them in turn for one priority. Tom took the floor first and spoke for nearly three full minutes about cost. Halfway through, Sara tried to add a comment, but Tom carried on, saying that he had not finished. Sara sat back, clearly annoyed, while the rest of the panel waited in silence. When Tom finally handed over, the moderator thanked him, turned to Sara and said: Go ahead, but please keep it brief, because Leo has been waiting patiently for his turn.

prompt.es: Completa: «La discusión iba bien hasta que alguien intentó intervenir sin pedir turno.»

answer.text: chime

feedback.es: Chime in es intervenir en una conversación ya iniciada; jump in o cut in son variantes válidas, aunque cut in suena más brusco.

origin.text: The discussion was going well until a guest tried to ___ in without asking, and two people began to talk over each other.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura del autor sobre los moderadores que casi no intervienen?

choices.text: They are a safe choice, because a silent moderator can never be accused of bias.
They cause problems: the loudest guests end up deciding who speaks.
They are acceptable only when the guests already know one another.

feedback.es: Sostiene que la pasividad favorece al más ruidoso y deja sin voz al más prudente: para él moderar es repartir la palabra.

origin.text: Moderators are often praised for saying little. I disagree. A moderator who never steps in lets the loudest guest decide who speaks, and the quietest guest, who often has the most careful view, leaves without being heard. A good moderator is not silent; the skill lies in asking the right person to take the floor at the right moment.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Nadie debe hablar encima de un colega que todavía está hablando.»

answer.text: Nobody should talk over a colleague who is still speaking

feedback.es: Talk over + persona describe hablar mientras otro habla; who is still speaking explica por qué es una falta de cortesía.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué actitud muestra Sara tras la interrupción?

choices.text: Defensive: she claims that Tom gave her no chance to speak.
Apologetic, but she drops her point entirely to avoid more conflict.
Apologetic, but still keen to add a short point.

feedback.es: Se disculpa y reconoce que Tom tenía derecho a mantener la palabra, pero aun así quiere aportar su cifra con cortesía.

origin.audio: Sorry, Tom, I should not have talked over you. You were right to hold the floor, and I will wait for my turn. Having said that, if you would not mind, I have one short figure that may save us some time.

prompt.es: ¿Por qué elige la moderadora al estudiante del fondo?

choices.text: She gives priority to the person who has waited longest without interrupting.
She prefers him to the other two because his question is better.
She assumes that a student is less likely to ask a difficult question.

feedback.es: La espera paciente del estudiante, frente a las otras dos manos levantadas, sugiere que la moderadora premia a quien respeta el turno.

origin.text: When the moderator said that there was time for one more question, three hands went up at once. She looked at the back of the room, where a student had been waiting politely for twenty minutes, and said: Yes, you, please go ahead.

title.en: Steer the panel back on track

es: Interrumpir con cortesía, pedir aclaraciones y reconducir una mesa redonda con fórmulas como Sorry to cut in, If I could just… y Coming back to….

teaching.en: Sorry to cut in, but could I clarify one figure before the discussion moves any further?
teaching.es: Perdona que te corte, pero ¿podría aclarar una cifra antes de que la discusión avance más?
teaching.explanationEs: Sorry to + verbo base (cut in) es la disculpa breve; could I + verbo base pide permiso con suavidad.
segments: Sorry to cut in, but could I clarify
one figure before the discussion moves any further?
teaching.audioText: Sorry to cut in, but could I clarify one figure before the discussion moves any further?

teaching.en: If I could just rephrase the question, I think it would be easier for every guest to answer.
teaching.es: Si pudiera reformular la pregunta, creo que sería más fácil de responder para todos los invitados.
teaching.explanationEs: If I could just + verbo pide permiso para hacer algo breve; el modal could lo vuelve cortés.
segments: If I could just rephrase the question, I think
it would be easier for every guest to answer.
teaching.audioText: If I could just rephrase the question, I think it would be easier for every guest to answer.

teaching.en: Can I just check that this is directly relevant, or are you about to go off on a tangent?
teaching.es: ¿Puedo comprobar si esto es directamente pertinente, o está a punto de irse por las ramas?
teaching.explanationEs: Can I just check…? suaviza la duda; go off on a tangent es alejarse del tema principal.
segments: Can I just check that this is directly relevant, or
are you about to go off on a tangent?
teaching.audioText: Can I just check that this is directly relevant, or are you about to go off on a tangent?

teaching.en: Coming back to the budget, could we clarify who pays and pin down the exact figure?
teaching.es: Volviendo al presupuesto, ¿podríamos aclarar quién paga y concretar la cifra exacta?
teaching.explanationEs: Coming back to + tema reconduce sin reproche; pin down exige una respuesta precisa.
segments: Coming back to the budget, could we clarify
who pays and pin down the exact figure?
teaching.audioText: Coming back to the budget, could we clarify who pays and pin down the exact figure?

teaching.en: To put it another way, a moderator who wants to redirect the debate should do so without blaming anyone.
teaching.es: Dicho de otro modo, un moderador que quiera reconducir el debate debe hacerlo sin culpar a nadie.
teaching.explanationEs: To put it another way introduce una reformulación; redirect significa dar otra dirección a la conversación.
segments: To put it another way, a moderator who wants to
redirect the debate should do so without blaming anyone.
teaching.audioText: To put it another way, a moderator who wants to redirect the debate should do so without blaming anyone.

teaching.en: Thank you for that comment; I will take that on board and check the figures again tonight.
teaching.es: Gracias por ese comentario; lo tendré en cuenta y revisaré las cifras otra vez esta noche.
teaching.explanationEs: Take that on board muestra que aceptas una observación sin ponerte a la defensiva.
segments: Thank you for that comment; I will take that
on board and check the figures again tonight.
teaching.audioText: Thank you for that comment; I will take that on board and check the figures again tonight.

prompt.es: Completa: «Perdona que te corte, pero ¿puedo aclarar una cifra?»

answer.text: cut

feedback.es: Sorry to cut in es la disculpa estándar antes de interrumpir; chime in y jump in son variantes válidas.

hint.es: Es el verbo que forma con in el verbo compuesto para interrumpir.

origin.text: Two guests were already speaking at once about the figures. Sorry to ___ in, but could I clarify one of them?

prompt.es: ¿Qué intervención reconduce la conversación?

choices.text: Coming back to the budget, could we settle who pays?
Holidays matter too, so let us leave the budget for another day.
That is an interesting tangent, so let us follow it for a while.

feedback.es: Coming back to… vuelve al tema central; las otras dos son amables, pero no reconducen: aplazan el presupuesto o siguen la digresión.

hint.es: Busca la frase que devuelve la conversación al tema, no la que la deja seguir.

origin.text: We were discussing the school budget, but for the last five minutes the conversation has drifted towards summer holidays.

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Podrías precisar la cifra exacta para nosotros?»

answer.text: Could you pin down the exact figure for us

feedback.es: Could you + verbo base forma la petición cortés; pin down pide una respuesta concreta.

hint.es: Empieza con la petición cortés Could you.

prompt.es: Completa: «Si pudiera reformularla, creo que todos la entenderíamos mejor.»

answer.text: rephrase

feedback.es: If I could just + verbo pide permiso para reformular con brevedad; reword y restate son sinónimos válidos.

origin.text: Your question is long, and I am not sure everyone followed it. If I could just ___ it, I think we would all understand it better.

prompt.es: ¿Qué intervención pide precisión a Mia con cortesía?

choices.text: Would you mind speaking more slowly so that we can follow?
Could you pin down which of those things matters most?
Could we move on, since none of that seems relevant?

feedback.es: Pide concretar cuál de los factores pesa más, sin reproche; las otras dos son corteses pero piden otra cosa: ritmo o cambiar de tema.

origin.text: Mia: Well, it depends on the budget, and on a few other things, and on what the parents think, although that is hard to say.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué hace el orador con sus primeras palabras?

choices.text: He politely interrupts to correct someone's figures.
He politely asks the moderator to change the topic.
He politely interrupts to explain his own point again.

feedback.es: Se disculpa, interrumpe y reformula su propia idea con «put it another way»: corrige un malentendido sobre lo que quiso decir.

origin.audio: Sorry to cut in, but that is not quite what I meant. If I could just put it another way, the real issue is not the money but the time that teachers need to learn the new system.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué hace Leo después de la intervención de Sara?

choices.text: He admits his digression and agrees to verify the numbers.
He defends his story and insists that the phone matters to the debate.
He asks Sara to give him two more minutes to finish his story.

feedback.es: Leo se ríe, reconoce que se fue por las ramas y promete comprobar las cifras.

origin.audio: The debate on school tablets had been calm until Leo began describing his cousin's new phone. Two minutes later he was still talking about its camera. Sara, who was leading the panel, waited for a pause and said: Sorry to cut in, Leo, but is this directly relevant to our budget? Leo laughed and admitted that he had gone off on a tangent. Sara thanked him and continued: Coming back to the budget, could you pin down how much a class set of tablets would cost? Leo said that he would check the figures and take that on board before the next session.

prompt.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué da a entender la pregunta de Sara sobre los comentarios de Leo?

choices.text: She believes they are relevant, but wants Leo to state them more briefly.
She doubts that they belong to the topic but avoids blaming him.
She suspects that they are meant to delay the discussion on purpose.

feedback.es: Formula una pregunta en lugar de una orden: deja ver su duda sobre la pertinencia sin culpar a Leo.

origin.audio: The debate on school tablets had been calm until Leo began describing his cousin's new phone. Two minutes later he was still talking about its camera. Sara, who was leading the panel, waited for a pause and said: Sorry to cut in, Leo, but is this directly relevant to our budget? Leo laughed and admitted that he had gone off on a tangent. Sara thanked him and continued: Coming back to the budget, could you pin down how much a class set of tablets would cost? Leo said that he would check the figures and take that on board before the next session.

prompt.es: Completa las tres intervenciones: interrumpir, comprobar y reformular.

answer.text: cut | check | rephrase

feedback.es: Las tres fórmulas corteses llevan verbo base: cut in para interrumpir, check para confirmar y rephrase para reformular.

sentences: Sorry to ___ in, but I have a question about the figure.
Can I just ___ that you mean the budget and not the cost of repairs?
If I could just ___ that, I think it would be clearer to the parents.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la opinión del autor sobre la reconducción cortés?

choices.text: It is worthwhile only when the moderator knows the guest well.
It is unfair to the guest but necessary for the audience.
It respects everyone involved, including the guest who drifts.

feedback.es: Defiende que reconducir con tacto protege al público, al que está siendo ignorado y hasta al propio invitado que divaga.

origin.text: Many panel moderators fear the word no. They let a guest drift from the subject because stopping him feels rude. I think the opposite is true. A polite way to redirect the talk, such as coming back to our question, protects the speaker who is being ignored, the audience who came for the topic, and, in the end, the guest who drifted, who would rather be stopped gently than be remembered for rambling.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Volviendo a la pregunta principal, ¿qué decidimos?»

answer.text: Coming back to the main question, what do we decide
accepted: Coming back to the main question, what do we decide
What do we decide, coming back to the main question

feedback.es: Coming back to + tema abre la frase que reconduce, y luego va la pregunta.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué quiere conseguir el orador con su pregunta final?

choices.text: A precise date instead of a vague promise.
Confirmation that Mia accepts the criticism she has just heard.
A reason to delay the decision until next year.

feedback.es: Pide concretar «soon» entre dos fechas posibles: busca precisión donde ella fue vaga.

origin.audio: Thank you for that comment, Mia. I will take that on board. But may I pin down one thing? When you say soon, do you mean this term or next year?

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender el orador sobre el plan?

choices.text: That it should be postponed until a cheaper plan is found.
That it may go wrong for the same reason as an earlier one.
That it is sound and only needs a better budget.

feedback.es: No dice que el plan sea malo, pero quiere comprobar que no se repite «the mistake of last year»: insinúa un riesgo conocido.

origin.text: I am not saying that the plan is bad. I am saying that nobody has yet explained who will pay for it, and I would like to check that we are not repeating the mistake of last year.

title.es: Resumir lo que dijeron los demás

es: Resumir las posturas de otros participantes con verbos de cita precisos (stressed, doubted, warned, insisted, suggested) y colocaciones como concede a point o cast doubt on.

vocabulary.es: admitir que el otro tiene razón en algo

teaching.en: Tom stressed that free buses would help poorer families most, but he did not play down the risks.
teaching.es: Tom subrayó que los autobuses gratuitos ayudarían sobre todo a las familias más pobres, pero no restó importancia a los riesgos.
teaching.explanationEs: Stressed marca lo que el hablante considera esencial; play down es lo contrario: quitar importancia.
segments: Tom stressed that free buses would help poorer families
most, but he did not play down the risks.
teaching.audioText: Tom stressed that free buses would help poorer families most, but he did not play down the risks.

teaching.en: Sara doubted that the city could afford the scheme, and she cast doubt on the figures in the report.
teaching.es: Sara dudó de que la ciudad pudiera permitirse el plan, y puso en duda las cifras del informe.
teaching.explanationEs: Doubted that + pasado resume el escepticismo; cast doubt on se aplica al objeto que se cuestiona.
segments: Sara doubted that the city could afford the scheme, and
she cast doubt on the figures in the report.
teaching.audioText: Sara doubted that the city could afford the scheme, and she cast doubt on the figures in the report.

teaching.en: Carlos warned that costs could rise, but he was ready to concede a point and to freely admit the idea was good.
teaching.es: Carlos advirtió de que los costos podían subir, pero estaba dispuesto a admitir un punto y a reconocer abiertamente que la idea era buena.
teaching.explanationEs: Concede a point y freely admit muestran una concesión: el hablante reconoce lo bueno del otro lado.
segments: Carlos warned that costs could rise, but he was ready to
concede a point and to freely admit the idea was good.
teaching.audioText: Carlos warned that costs could rise, but he was ready to concede a point and to freely admit the idea was good.

teaching.en: Mia insisted that we must start this year, and she was ready to argue the case for acting at once.
teaching.es: Mia insistió en que debíamos empezar este año, y estaba dispuesta a defender la conveniencia de actuar de inmediato.
teaching.explanationEs: Insisted that + oración: no lleva preposición (insisted on solo precede a un sustantivo o a un verbo en -ing).
segments: Mia insisted that we must start this year, and she
was ready to argue the case for acting at once.
teaching.audioText: Mia insisted that we must start this year, and she was ready to argue the case for acting at once.

teaching.en: Ana suggested that we test it in one district; she was happy to float the idea of a short trial first.
teaching.es: Ana sugirió que lo probáramos en un distrito; estaba contenta de lanzar la idea de una prueba breve antes.
teaching.explanationEs: Suggested that we + verbo base propone una acción; float the idea la presenta como un globo de ensayo.
segments: Ana suggested that we test it in one district; she was
happy to float the idea of a short trial first.
teaching.audioText: Ana suggested that we test it in one district; she was happy to float the idea of a short trial first.

teaching.en: Some guests were bound to take issue with the plan, so the moderator suggested that they name each objection in turn.
teaching.es: Era inevitable que algunos invitados discreparan del plan, así que la moderadora sugirió que nombraran cada objeción por turno.
teaching.explanationEs: Take issue with + algo expresa desacuerdo abierto; es más fuerte que disagree.
segments: Some guests were bound to take issue with the plan, so
the moderator suggested that they name each objection in turn.
teaching.audioText: Some guests were bound to take issue with the plan, so the moderator suggested that they name each objection in turn.

prompt.es: Elige el resumen fiel de lo que dijo Leo.

choices.text: Leo doubted that the plan deserved a trial.
Leo conceded that the plan was not perfect.
Leo suggested that the plan be dropped at once.

feedback.es: «You are right» y «the plan is not perfect» muestran una concesión abierta: conceded resume ese reconocimiento.

hint.es: Leo reconoce algo incómodo, pero mantiene su apoyo.

origin.text: Leo: You are right, the plan is not perfect, and I will say so openly, but I still think it deserves our support.

prompt.es: Completa: «Carlos advirtió de que los costos podían duplicarse.»

answer.text: warned

feedback.es: Warned that + riesgo futuro resume un aviso; cautioned es un sinónimo más formal.

hint.es: Es el verbo que resume un aviso sobre un peligro futuro.

origin.text: Carlos ___ that costs could double within two years, so he urged the panel to plan carefully.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Tom se negó a quitar importancia a los riesgos del plan.»

answer.text: Tom refused to play down the risks of the plan

feedback.es: Refused to + verbo base expresa rechazo; play down es quitar importancia, y aquí se niega.

hint.es: El sujeto es Tom y el verbo de rechazo va después.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cómo resumirías lo que dijo Carlos?

choices.text: He admitted that the bill had already doubled for some families.
He doubted that careful planning would change what families pay.
He warned that careless planning could make the bill twice as high.

feedback.es: El aviso de un riesgo futuro (la factura podría duplicarse) se resume con warned.

origin.audio: If we do not plan carefully, costs could double within two years, and the families who already struggle will be the ones who pay for it.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cómo resumirías la postura de la oradora?

choices.text: She insisted that the work begin before the year ends.
She suggested that the work might begin within the year.
She conceded that the work could wait another year.

feedback.es: Rechaza otra fecha y mantiene su exigencia con firmeza: insisted, no suggested ni admitted.

origin.audio: I will not accept a later date. We have waited long enough, and if the council will not start this year, I will keep asking until it does.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada expresión con lo que hace el hablante.

cast doubt on a claim
float the idea of a trial

concede a point

pairs.es: Admitir que el otro tiene razón en algo

feedback.es: Cada colocación matiza la postura: restar importancia, dudar, proponer, discrepar o conceder.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿quién puso en duda la encuesta de la biblioteca?

choices.text: Luna, who refused to play down the benefits of opening on Sundays.
Rex, who doubted that the council could pay for extra staff.
Sol, who admitted that Sundays would cost the council a great deal.

feedback.es: Fue Rex quien «took issue with the survey»; Luna subrayó los beneficios y Sol admitió el costo.

origin.audio: Four guests discussed whether the town library should open on Sundays. Luna stressed that working families have no other free day, and she refused to play down the benefits. Rex doubted that the council could pay for extra staff, and he took issue with the survey that the library had published. Sol freely admitted that Sundays were expensive, but she insisted that books were a public service. The moderator then floated the idea of a six-month trial, and all four guests said that they could live with that, provided the results were published.

choices.text: That they had finally settled their disagreement about the cost of opening.
That they all wanted the library to open every single Sunday without delay.
That they would accept a trial if its results were made public.

feedback.es: Aceptan la prueba «provided the results were published»: una aceptación condicionada, no un acuerdo sobre el costo.

answer.text: Thank you, Leo. I take your point, and I agree with you up to a point. Tablets are light, they are cheap to update, and a child can carry a whole library in one bag. But I see one drawback in a complete switch: many pupils read more slowly on a screen, and they get distracted by notifications. For instance, last month my teacher asked us to read a short story on a tablet, and half of the class ended up checking messages. Building on your idea, I would suggest a simple compromise: tablets for research and exercises, and paper for long reading. Furthermore, we could ask pupils to help us write the rules, because people follow what they choose. That is partly why I would not remove paper completely. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they read better on paper or on a screen? I would like to hear your view before we decide anything.
accepted: Thank you, Leo. I take your point, and I agree with you up to a point. Tablets are light, they are cheap to update, and a child can carry a whole library in one bag. Furthermore, we could ask pupils to help us write the rules, because people follow what they choose. That is partly why I would not remove paper completely. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they read better on paper or on a screen? I would like to hear your view before we decide anything.

Thanks, Leo. That is a fair point, and to a certain extent I agree with you, because tablets really do save a lot of weight and money. However, I see one problem: a screen makes it easy to open something else. For example, yesterday I tried to read a chapter on my tablet and I answered four messages before the end of the first page. Expanding on your idea, I would like to propose that every school keeps a set of paper books for long reading, and uses tablets for everything else. I would add that pupils should choose the books themselves, because a child reads more when the book belongs to them. Mia, what is your experience with the youngest pupils? Would the same plan work for them, or do they need something different? I am curious about your view, and I would like to hear it before we make any decision.

origin.audio: Homework builds habits, and I agree with Leo up to a point. But for some pupils it only adds stress, and I have seen that with my own eyes. Take the case of my neighbour's son: he finishes his homework at ten at night and then cannot sleep. Furthermore, the teachers who set the most homework rarely have time to mark it properly, so the effort often disappears without a word of feedback. So I would not remove homework completely; I would reduce it, and I would make sure that every task counts for something.

answer.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to tonight's panel. Our topic is technology in the classroom. Let me introduce our three panellists: Ana, who uses tablets every day; Tom, who teaches science; and Sara, who has three children at school. Ana, would you like to start? Thank you, Ana. Tom, it is your turn. Sorry to cut in, Tom, but coming back to the main question, could you pin down the cost? Thank you. Before we move on, let me draw the threads together. Ana stressed that tablets saved time. Tom doubted that schools could afford them, and he warned that screens could distract pupils. Sara suggested that we write clear rules, and she conceded that tablets had real benefits. Sara, what would your first rule be? Seldom have I seen three guests agree on so much. To wrap up, all of you agree that rules matter more than machines. I am deeply grateful to each panellist for a lively discussion, and I thank our audience for listening. Good night, everyone.

feedback.es: «For once» sugiere que lo habitual es terminar en disputa: valora que esta mesa acabara con un plan.

origin.audio: Near the end of the panel, the moderator summed up: Ana stressed that tablets save time, Tom doubted that schools can afford them, and Sara suggested writing clear rules. Then she asked whether that was a fair summary. Tom nodded, but added that he would support tablets if the council published the real costs. Ana said that she could live with that, and Sara reminded everyone that rules cost nothing. The moderator smiled, thanked all three, and said that, for once, a panel on technology had ended with a plan instead of a quarrel.

prompt.es: Completa: «Su tarea era mantener la discusión encauzada y ser justa con todos.»

answer.text: keep

feedback.es: Keep the discussion on track es la colocación que describe la tarea central de quien modera.

origin.text: The moderator did not give her own opinion. Her job was to ___ the discussion on track and to give every panellist a fair hearing.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Estoy profundamente agradecido a cada ponente por la discusión de esta noche.»

answer.text: I am deeply grateful to each panellist for tonight's discussion

feedback.es: Deeply grateful to + persona dirige el agradecimiento, y for + sustantivo indica el motivo.

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender el autor sobre los resúmenes descuidados?

choices.text: That they tend to give too much time to the guest who spoke last.
That guests rarely notice any real difference between the two versions.
That they may soften a guest's position to please the room.

feedback.es: Advierte que un resumen debe ser fiel aunque incomode: sugiere que el descuido tiende a suavizar la postura de alguien para agradar.

origin.text: A summary is not a vote. When a moderator draws the threads together, she must not choose the most comfortable version of what each guest said. If Sara doubted the plan, the summary says that she doubted it, even if the room would prefer to hear that she had merely asked a question.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué valora más la moderadora al cerrar?

choices.text: The polite way in which the guests disagreed.
The passion with which the guests defended their views.
The number of people who came to the session.

feedback.es: Da las gracias sobre todo a los ponentes «who disagreed with great courtesy»: valora la cortesía en el desacuerdo.

origin.audio: Our time is up. Thank you for coming, and thank you most of all to our panellists, who disagreed with great courtesy, which is rarer than people think.
